sentences: The wealthy man, capitalist, stands in the library of his home at midnight and savagely denounces someone who cannot be seen, declaring that he will immediately take steps to put his enemy in the hands of the police.
As he reaches for the phone, he is struck down and falls to the floor, murdered, his attacker gone.
The housemaid, the maid; the manservant, the butler; the ward, the adopted daughter; and the older lady, her companion, all rush into the room to find the wealthy man dead.
The son, estranged from his father for months but who had been at the latter's home the evening of the murder, arrives the next morning.
He is soon followed by the investigator, a clever detective whom the son engages to investigate the elder man's death.

Not only the son but also the servants are impelled to suspect the ward of the crime, since the son's quarrel with his father had induced the elder man to restore the son's inheritance, thereby taking the fortune away from the ward.
All, however, wish to protect her.
On the arrival of the detective, accompanied by the first assistant and the second assistant, his assistants, all members of the household are detected in deceptive acts and statements.
The investigator's suspicion of the ward increases when she refuses to have her fingerprints taken, though he obtains them later by a ruse.
The ward, in turn, suspects the son may be guilty, and both she and the son endeavor to protect each other.
They meet for a moment in the house, and the investigator overhears them making statements indicating guilty knowledge of the crime.
The lawyer, former attorney for the wealthy man and a permanent guest at his home, cooperates with the investigator in attempting to solve the mystery.
In his investigations, the investigator finds a counterfeit five hundred dollar bill in a drawer of the library table.

He learns that the woman from the past (corrected from a misspelt name) was associated with the wealthy man's life 20 years before; was involved with the notorious master forger's gang of counterfeiters; and was imprisoned.
Though the master forger has been thought dead for 20 years, treasury officials declare that the only man who could have produced so perfect a counterfeit is the same master forger.
The investigator suspects the lawyer of complicity in the crime, though tangible evidence is lacking.

Since the woman from the past is allegedly mentioned in the wealthy man's will, the investigator advertises for her, and she appears at his office revealing herself now as the landlady, keeper of a boarding house.
The investigator warns the landlady that the ward is suspected publicly and plans to shield her from reporters.
To aid his trap, the ward must appear to have run away, so the landlady takes the ward to her boarding house against the ward's wishes.
The ward agrees to go believing this act will help protect the son.
While the landlady is out, the investigator's men install dictaphones in every room of the boarding house.
Radio operatives the first assistant and the second assistant monitor the wires from an attic of the house next door, able to listen to everything said in the boarding house.
During the surveillance, the investigator overhears talk regarding the master forger, and later hears the lawyer, who has gone to the house and seems on friendly terms with its occupants.
The gangster, a member of the gang, grows suspicious of the ward and is about to eject her but is stopped by the investigator and his men.
The detective reveals to the landlady that he knows her to be the ward's mother and the missing woman from the past.
The lawyer escapes from the house, unaware that the ward is the new roomer.
With the lawyer and the landlady face to face, the investigator plays one against the other, bringing out that they are married and that the lawyer is, in fact, the master forger himself.
It is finally established that the lawyer killed the wealthy man when threatened with exposure.
The lawyer is arrested for murder, and the picture closes with the investigator and the ward in each other's arms.
The adventurer, a demobilised British captain bored with civilian life, places a personal advertisement in the newspaper offering his services for "any excitement".
One of the many replies intrigues him: the young woman claims she is in great danger.
He immediately sets out for the country inn, where she has reserved some rooms for him.
Unable to persuade him to give up this mad adventure, his friend the idle gentleman follows after, dragging the adventurer's valet, the manservant, along.
The young woman turns out to be all the adventurer had hoped for: beautiful and desperately in need of help.

Her wealthy uncle, the invalid, is being treated in a hospital by a sinister doctor for a nervous breakdown, but she is sure there is something wrong about the hospital and the sinister doctor, and that she is being watched constantly.
She runs away when she spots the outline of two eavesdropping men (the idle gentleman and the manservant), much to the adventurer's annoyance.
She is caught and taken to the sinister doctor's nursing home by the gang leader, the adventuress and the doctor.
When the adventurer follows, he witnesses the invalid's unsuccessful attempt to escape.
The adventurer drives away, but returns stealthily and rescues the young woman.

Sending her off with the idle gentleman and the manservant, he sneaks back once more and overhears the adventuress convince the others to stay and try to get the invalid's signature on a document transferring securities and jewels to them.
The adventurer manages to save the invalid.
However, he makes a serious error when he takes the invalid back to the inn.
The villains soon arrive there.
The adventurer manages to disguise himself as the invalid; the crooks take him back, along with the young woman.
When they realise they have the wrong man they threaten to torture the young woman.
The adventurer tells them the invalid is hidden at the inn (whereas he is really being driven to the capital).
While the gang leader and the adventuress go to check, the adventurer is freed by the young woman before the sinister doctor can kill him.
He strangles the doctor.
The adventurer disarms the gang leader when he returns, but his gang pose as policemen and take him away.
The young woman persuades the adventurer to let them go, telling him she loves him.

The gentleman is happy when his son the young man breaks off his affair with conniving showgirl the performer – known as "the singer" – and reconciles his engagement with her co-star and neighbor the fiancée.
The gentleman goes to see the singer to bribe her to leave the young man alone, but she declines his offer; she wishes to marry the young man to further her ambitions of joining the social elite.
She threatens to reveal the young man's embezzlement from the elder gentleman's bank if the young man marries the fiancée, and despite his pleading, refuses to negotiate.

After the gentleman leaves, she telephones two club patrons she has been blackmailing, the first patron and the second patron, to demand one final generous gift from each of them by the next day; she makes the same request of "creepy" admirer the physician.
Her former husband the burglar – who has broken out of prison and into her apartment and has overheard her phone calls – demands half of the blackmail.
She refuses to give him anything, even after he hits her.
The following night around midnight, the gentleman visits her again, but is again unable to change her mind.
After he reaches the lobby of her building, he and another person hear screams from her place.
They knock on the door, but she assures them that she is fine.
The first patron, the second patron and the physician are all shown lurking about her apartment building late that night.
The singer is found strangled the next day; the coroner places the time of death around midnight.
The prosecutor investigates, aided by the gentleman's close friend the detective, and the sergeant.
After all the suspects are brought in for questioning, the detective asks the prosecutor to keep them waiting for a few hours.
The detective subtly maneuvers the first patron, the second patron, the physician and the two gentlemen into playing poker to pass the time so he can observe their personality traits.
Only the elder gentleman shows the daring, imagination and discipline required for the crime; the gentleman bluffs the detective, betting everything with just a pair of deuces.
Upon the production of a photograph of the burglar, the man who witnessed the performer's murder, the suspects are released.
The burglar, who witnessed the murder while hiding in the closet, sends the killer several blackmail letters.
He too is strangled.
A pen found at the scene has the young man's name on it, so the sergeant arrests him for the murder.
The young man then confesses to both murders, but the detective knows better.
He telephones the gentleman with the news and suggests they meet in an hour.
The gentleman speeds to the city from his country estate to confess, but his chauffeur makes a fatal mistake by trying to beat a train to a crossing, and the gentleman is killed.
Now the detective has to show how the gentleman murdered the singer in order to free the young man.
He is able to prove that the singer was dead before the gentleman left her apartment that night.
The gentleman had made a recording (the detective speculates it was the gentleman himself pretending to be the woman) to fool a stuttering witness into believing the singer was alive after her death.
The recording is found in the apartment, and the young man is released.
The scoundrel is a gambler, womanizer, and con man whose luck has run out.
Losing heavily at the track, he owes large sums to a clique of gamblers who have grown impatient with his refusal to pay.
They decide he must be eliminated, assigning the job to the henchman, a smooth but dangerous associate.
The scoundrel's personal life is no less tangled.
At the estate of retired sea captain the host, the scoundrel is conducting an affair with the Captain's young second wife, the stepmother, an ex-actress who married for comfort rather than love.
The scoundrel is also ending a relationship with the maid, one of the estate's maids, who still loves him but now harbors resentment.
When the scoundrel tries to extort money from the stepmother to keep her husband from learning of their affair, she refuses.
Their confrontation makes her another potential enemy.
The young woman, the host's daughter from his first marriage, is in love with the suitor, a solid young man with a jealous streak.
The suitor has come to believe the scoundrel is visiting the young woman.
The stepmother cannot tell him the truth—that she is the one the scoundrel meets—without risking a scandal that would wound her husband.
One night, the suitor sees the stepmother, cloaked in the young woman's wrap, rendezvous with the scoundrel.
Mistaking her for the young woman, he follows the scoundrel, beats him, and threatens to kill him if he ever comes near “the young woman” again.
On the night of the host's birthday dinner, the Captain—his suspicions about the scoundrel and his wife now strong—slips a revolver into his pocket before greeting guests.
Among the arrivals are the henchman, the suitor, the young woman, the stepmother, and various friends.
The manservant, the quiet but observant butler, oversees the serving.
During dinner, the scoundrel amuses the company with the story of his peculiar cat's-eye ring, said to hypnotize women and glow in the dark.
Skepticism runs around the table.
The scoundrel invites a demonstration, and on the host's order, the manservant extinguishes the lights.
The greenish glow of the ring draws exclamations—then a shadow blocks it.
A groan, a crash of cutlery, and a body slump in the dark.
When the lights come on, the scoundrel is dead—slumped in his chair, a carving knife buried between his shoulders.
The doctor, a guest, pronounces him dead.
The inspector and his assistant the junior officer arrive.
In the babble of overlapping accusations, the inspector calls for order and searches the guests.
A revolver is found on the henchman.
Recognizing the henchman's criminal past, the inspector suspects him of the killing.
The henchman denies it but says he can point to the murderer.
The inspector demands the cat's-eye ring, but it is missing—until, to his surprise, it turns up in his own pocket.
The henchman remarks on the extraordinary brightness of the ring in darkness.
The inspector is skeptical, and to test it, orders the lights turned out again while the henchman begins his revelation.
In the dark, the henchman resumes his account.
Mid-sentence, he gasps and falls silent.
The lights snap on—the henchman is dead, stabbed with the same carving knife.
The ring has once again disappeared.
The inspector's fury grows: two murders under his very nose.
A policeman returns from the scoundrel's apartment with fragments of a letter in a woman's hand.
The inspector orders the manservant to piece them together, but the manservant discreetly palms some scraps.
The inspector then has all the women write sample lines for comparison; the manservant switches one slip to prevent a match.
Outside, the groundskeeper, the wooden-legged gardener, is caught snooping.
From his private balcony, elderly Prof.
The professor and his servant see the body of family friend the first victim with an arrow in his chest.
The professor calls district attorney the prosecutor, who brings in private detective the sleuth and lazy police detective the policeman.
The sleuth quickly deduces that the arrow scene was staged (the first victim was actually bludgeoned inside the house), but there is no obvious suspect.
Living with the professor is his niece the young woman; the professor's adopted son, the young man, who is also the young woman's boyfriend, returns from college on hearing of the crime.
In the next house are the neighbors, a brother and sister: she feels responsible for a serious injury he still suffers from, and is now frail and agoraphobic.
She could have seen the body from her window, and the brother says he heard her screaming in her room; she fearfully says she saw nothing and did not scream.
The brother admits to being in the professor's house before the murder.
Another neighbor is the chess player, a chess enthusiast, who seems overly interested in the case.
A taunting typewritten note is found, signed "the Bishop".
It alludes to the nursery rhyme "a rhyme about a slain bird".
That was the first victim's nickname, and another visitor at the house that day was named the visitor's surname—German for "Sparrow"—but he proves to have a solid alibi.
Neither the brother's nor the young man's typewriter matches the note, and the professor does not have one.
Later a friend of the young man's, named a common first name, is found murdered.
He was shot in the top of the head, an allusion to the boy's injury in "a rhyme about two children".
Then the brother, sitting on a low wall in a park at night, is pulled off the wall and murdered: like "the nursery-rhyme egg", says a note from "the Bishop".
The brother's sister is found dead also, perhaps from fright, with a chess bishop in her hand; a valuable notebook about the brother's research work is missing from their home.

The policeman and the prosecutor become suspicious of the chess player, but find him dead, along with a house of cards (obviously built after he died) with a chess bishop on top: "a rhyme about a house".
Later, the professor expresses some misgivings about the young man, and mentions the playwright's play the drama, which the young man is fond of.
That night, after the young woman says goodnight to the young man, she makes her way into the attic and finds the typewriter that "the Bishop" used for his notes.
At this point she is jumped from behind.
Mulling over the professor's words later that night, the sleuth suddenly realizes that one of the characters in the drama is a bishop—named the young man's surname.
He rushes back to the professor's house together with the prosecutor, the policeman, and more police.
The young man's window is open and neither he nor the young woman is in their room.
The professor joins the group to search the house.
Breaking down the locked door to the attic, they find the typewriter, but not the young woman, who is bound and gagged in a nearby cupola.
Downstairs, they are talking to the professor when the young man returns.
When the sleuth accuses him, he acts guilty.
Meanwhile, the professor surreptitiously pours some powder from a poison ring into a wine glass.
As things calm down and the young man is about to be arrested, the professor pours wine for the young man and himself; but the sleuth announces that he has switched the glasses.
The professor is the murderer, and was trying to fake the young man's suicide.
He was jealous and wanted to be the young woman's only friend.
He originally only intended to kill the first victim and frame the young man, but developed the more elaborate scheme when he realized the sister must have witnessed his actions.
The young man acted guilty because the sleuth asked him to.
And the young woman is fine; after the professor left the attic, the sleuth had asked the policeman to search the cupola.
The young man and the young woman embrace.
The sleuth stops the policeman from carelessly drinking the poison.
The socialite is married to the tycoon, an unpleasant millionaire, who is constantly cheating on her.
Being fed up with his affairs, the socialite, who is in love with the suitor, asks the tycoon for a divorce but he constantly refuses.
The tycoon's lawyer, manages to prevent her from filing for divorce for a while.
One evening, at a dinner party given by the host, the socialite announces that her husband has finally granted her a divorce.
The suitor, however, is disappointed to find that she did not ask for a settlement or alimony.
Later, the young man, the socialite's son, discovered that his father had been murdered with poison and accuses the suitor of the deed and chastises his mother for protecting him.
The tycoon' s lawyer accuses the suitor of being a penniless fortune-hunter.
This further blackens the case again the suitor.
The physician, who is the family doctor. is also suspected because of his unusual interest in the socialite.
The socialite is also a suspect because she seems distraught during the dinner party, which occurred on the night that the tycoon was murdered.
The socialite at first quarrels with the family friend and orders him out of her house.
Later on she turns to him for help.
He at first seem uninterested in helping, but when he discovers that the socialite is not in love with the suitor, he agrees to help her.
The family friend then locks the apartment door and begins to discuss the case.
The socialite's loyal servants are coached in their testimony by the family friend but they are unable to remember their lines.
After an intensive investigation of suspects in the death of the tycoon, the family friend breaks down and confesses to the crime.
The family friend declares his love for the socialite, but is rejected and commits suicide by falling out of a window.
A murder is supposedly caused by a gorilla.
Police catch only a glimpse of a gorilla's shadow, cast against a brick wall, before it disappears.
When the homeowner receives a note that the gorilla will arrive at his home before midnight, he hires detectives the first detective and the second detective to help protect him.
The homeowner lives with his ward, the young woman, who is in love with the suitor.
The first detective and the second detective stand guard outside the house until close to midnight, but do not see anything suspicious.
The second detective persuades the first detective to don a gorilla suit to entice the gorilla and trap him.
To avoid being shot by those searching for the gorilla, the first detective wears a white ribbon around his neck.
While the first detective searches for the gorilla, the real gorilla appears and chases the second detective, who climbs a tree and calls for help, but no one arrives.
The gorilla breaks off a branch of the tree and the second detective falls to the ground.
The gorilla then finds the first detective, who has hidden in another tree.
He reaches for the first detective, but simply removes the white ribbon and places it around his own neck.
The real gorilla then wanders freely, leaving the first detective, unable to remove his costume's head, hunted as the real gorilla.
The first detective finally removes the head, but is still pursued and shot at in the dark until he reaches a lighted area.
The suitor, who turns out to be an undercover detective, discovers that the homeowner, in a gorilla suit of his own, is the real murderer.
The young heir, a young wealthy big-city club-man is engaged to the fiancée, daughter of a national Senator.
The young heir is preparing to spend a weekend at the Senator's estate.
He becomes involved in the affairs of a gang of blackmailers through his efforts to help a fellow club member.
When the friend, a fellow club-member, arrives with a note, imprinted with a purple hieroglyph, in which he, the friend, is threatened with a horrible death.
Since the friend is nervous and terrified, the young heir agrees to stay with him at his apartment that night.
A little after midnight, the friend finally recovers his nerve and the young heir takes a cab home.
The next day a body, terribly mutilated beyond recognition is found.
Following the funeral, the doctor, accidentally smokes a poisoned cigarette.
The young heir, the fiancée, and the lieutenant, who claims to be in the secret service, take the doctor to his home for an antidote.
While searching for the antidote, the doctor's body disappears.
While they search for his body, they find footprints that lead to a slipper, inside of which they find another note with a purple hieroglyph.
Numerous other blackmail threats follow, demanding money from the young heir.
While at a Chinese garden party, the fiancée is kidnapped and a ransom is demanded from the young heir for her return.
While on his way to pay the ransom, the young heir is captured by the blackmailers in a speedboat, but a national submarine rescues both the young heir and the fiancée.
The criminals turn out to be none other than the friend, the doctor, and the lieutenant, who concocted the scheme to get money from the young heir.
The rogue is a jewel thief known as the "gentleman burglar", who falls in love with the sweetheart.
The rogue gets engaged to the sweetheart and gifts her his latest theft, a diamond bracelet.
He decides to give up his criminal ways until his friend the companion attempts a suicide, due to his inability to repay gambling debt.
The rogue offers to get him the needed money.
He asks to join the companion as a weekend guest of the nobleman and the noblewoman, intending to steal the celebrated family necklace.
Complications arise when a gang of thieves also has the same thing in mind.
Tipped off to their plan, the inspector of the police headquarters arrives at the family estate with his men.
Unexpectedly, the sweetheart shows up there and joins the rolling party.
Head burglar the gang leader breaks into the house and succeeds in stealing the necklace, only to have the rogue take it away.
The alarm is sounded and the gang leader is caught empty-handed by the police, but remains silent, hoping to settle his score yet with the rogue.
When and the necklace is not found in the house, the inspector confines all the guests to it, then quickly changes his mind.
The sweetheart, who has developed her own suspicions, overhears him tell one of his men that he intends to let the gang leader escape, expecting the crook to lead him to the rogue.
She follows the rogue back to the capital to warn him.
The inspector appears at the rogue’s home, finding the sweetheart in hiding in its guest room, “compromising” her reputation.
She learns the rogue has the necklace, but not why.
The gang leader shows up on the rogue’s rooftop, drawing the inspector away in chase.
The gang leader then appears and takes the rogue at gunpoint.
However, the rogue convinces him that it is too dangerous to flee with the necklace with all the policemen around and helps him escape.
Then, after a ruse put on by the rogue fails and the nobleman shows up, the inspector accuses the rogue of being the gentleman burglar.
Cornered and bound for jail, the rogue reminds the nobleman of the 1,000 pound reward he offered for the necklace's return.
Indicating only that the companion could use that amount, he then has his nonplussed friend produce and hand it over.
The nobleman presses for the matter to be dropped, but the inspector reveals the warrant he has for the rogue’s arrest is for the theft of a diamond bracelet.
Saying he is in no position to restore it the way he has the necklace, the rogue stands silent as the sweetheart removes it from her wrist and hands it to the inspector.
She declares herself compromised in front of a distraught nobleman, who leaves, dumbfounded and grumbling at the unsavory developments.
Springing another gambit, the rogue again outwits the inspector, and seeks to flee alone to the life of a perpetual fugitive.
The sweetheart interrupts him, professes her love in spite of knowing what he has done, still without knowing why, and promises to accompany him wherever their journey may lead.
Arranging to meet her in another city, the rogue makes a successful escape disguised in the inspector’s frock coat and hat.
The young man and the young woman, two American tourists in the city, meet each other at a city hotel while eating breakfast.
Both are reading the personal columns of the newspaper.
The next day the young man inserts an ad, under the alias of a mock nobleman's name, which requests her friendship.
The young woman, using the alias of a mock noblewoman's name, places an ad in reply which suggests that he should write a series of five letters proving himself worth knowing.
The young man makes up a fabulous story about a murder mystery based on the things he has heard his upstairs neighbors arguing about.
The young woman's aunt, who disapproves of the young man, suspects the young man is the murderer and contacts the police headquarters.
The young man's neighbor (the one he mentioned in his letters) is found dead and the police immediately suspect the young man and the young woman as being involved in the murder.
The real murderer, when he hears they are prime suspects, then attempts to frame them.
